20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;">The steps a request goes through inside the API layer</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These steps are repeated on each iteration of the loop. The inference is out of the API layer’s control. The API cannot make the GPU any faster. All it can do is add as little delay as possible around it. The time the API layer spends parsing, validating, or tokenizing is extra latency the user feels. </span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>How to make the API layer efficient?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenAI adopted the following techniques to reduce the overhead coming from different places in the API layer.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><span>1. Tokenizing only the delta</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Models do not read text. Before inference starts, the prompt must be converted into token IDs. Tokenizers convert the text into token IDs in O(n), linearly going over each token in the prompt and replacing it with the token ID. Under stateless HTTP, the whole conversation gets retokenized on every call. By the twentieth tool call, the API is rereading many thousands of tokens to extract one new result. The GPU only needs the new tool result, but the CPU is rereading the book from page one, and the cost keeps growing with input length.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With the WebSocket, the API keeps the tokenized conversation in server memory. The first request tokenizes the full prompt, but every later request sends only the new items. The API tokenizes just that piece and appends it to the stored sequence. This way, per-call tokenization stops depending on conversation length and becomes closer to O(1), depending on the length of the marginal input.</span></p><div calc(1.125em * 1);"><span>2. Running safety checks in parallel with inference</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Agents have to check each request for safety before showing the output to a user. OpenAI implemented safety checks in its API layer. Images go through their own classifiers, while the prompt text goes to classifier models that look for dangerous content, like cyberoffense or bioweapon instructions. These classifiers take time to run. The simple design is to run them first and start inference only after they pass. The problem is that this delay is added to the time-to-first-token (TTFT) of all requests, while the vast majority of them are completely harmless.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The fix is to run the safety checks and inference at the same time. The model takes some time to process the prompt before its first token comes out, so the checks use that window to finish. If a check fails, the API reacts depending on the model. For some models, it streams tokens to the user right away and cuts the stream when a check fails. For more sensitive models, it holds the output until the checks pass and only then releases it. In both cases, the time spent on safety hides inside a wait that was going to happen anyway.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><span>3. Routing traffic to newer CPUs</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When a company runs servers at scale, its fleet ends up with machines bought in different years, and therefore with different generations of CPUs. The scheduling software usually treats machines of the same type as identical. In reality, they are not. OpenAI queried Kubernetes for the actual processor model behind each of its deployments and found a mix of older Broadwell chips and newer Ice Lake chips behind the same machine labels. The older ones were serving the same traffic with roughly 20% worse time to first token, while using about twice as much CPU.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To fix this, OpenAI shifted more traffic toward the machines with newer processors and started treating CPU generation as an explicit factor in capacity planning. Sometimes the best software optimization is better hardware.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Inference Optimization</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The inference layer is where the model actually runs. There are fleets of GPUs and other accelerators, and the serving software (the engine) that operates them. The model’s core computation is enormous matrix arithmetic, which parallelizes across the thousands of cores an accelerator provides. The layer schedules and batches incoming requests across the fleet, holds the per-conversation state that generation depends on, executes the model’s forward passes, and hands each generated token back to the API layer.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>How to make the inference layer efficient?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Demand for tokens grows faster than hardware can be added, so at this layer slow and wasteful are the same word. The waste hides in four places: work routed to the wrong machine, memory holding the wrong state, parallel hardware idling through sequential generation, and two mismatched phases sharing the same machines.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenAI adopted the following techniques to make the inference layer more efficient.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><span>1. Balancing load with cache-aware routing</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenAI serves its models from many GPU machines. Every request has to be sent to one of them. If that routing is uneven, some machines sit idle while others queue up work. Idle GPUs are the most expensive kind of waste in the stack. There is also a second, less obvious problem. Each machine keeps the computed state (the cache) for the conversations it recently served. If the next request of a conversation lands on a different machine, that cache is useless. The new machine must recompute everything from scratch, even though the work already exists somewhere else.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So the router has two goals:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Spreading load evenly:</span></strong><span> send the request to the least busy machine.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Using the cache:</span></strong><span> send it back to the machine that already knows this conversation.</span></p></li></ol><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenAI’s routing weighs both for every request, along with basics like geography and available capacity. Improvements in load balancing alone have dramatically reduced the cost of serving its models.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><span>2. Managing the KV cache</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When a transformer generates a token, it attends over all previous tokens. To avoid recomputing that attention state for every new token, the serving system keeps it in accelerator memory, in what is called the KV cache. The cache grows linearly with conversation length, multiplied by every concurrent conversation the fleet is serving. For long contexts it can rival the size of the weights themselves. If the software evicts the wrong state, the inference layer pays the full processing cost again when that conversation returns.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The efficiency technique here is to manage the cache based on real usage. OpenAI analyzes production traces to learn which cached state is likely to be needed again, tests eviction policies against that data instead of intuition, and optimizes how cached state is stored and moved between memory tiers. This ensures the most valuable work stays around longer without running out of memory or wasting time moving data.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: Speculative decoding</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Generation is sequential. Each token depends on the previous one, so a model that processes a huge prompt in one parallel pass must produce its answer one token at a time. In large models, producing these tokens is expensive and slow, even when the next token is easy to guess. For an input like “the capital of France is”, the next token is almost certainly “Paris”, but the model still has to process the entire conversation and perform large matrix multiplications to predict it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Speculative decoding uses a small draft model to propose the next several tokens, and the large model verifies all of them in a single parallel pass. In many cases, the draft proposals are correct and will be accepted by the large model, which saves the time the large model would have taken to produce them one at a time. When a proposal is wrong, the large model discards it and produces its own token, so the output quality does not change. The main metric to evaluate the draft model is the average acceptance length, which is how many proposed tokens the main model accepts in each pass.</span></p><div Separating prefill and decode</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Inference has two phases, prefill and decode. Prefill processes the entire incoming prompt in one massively parallel pass, and it builds the internal state (KV cache) the model needs. Decode then generates the response one token at a time. These two are very different workloads. Prefill is compute-heavy, while decode is memory-heavy, spending most of its time streaming weights and cached state through memory. Running both on the same machines means neither runs on hardware set up for it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The efficiency technique is to separate them. One part of the fleet handles prefill and another handles decode, each configured for its own bottleneck. When a request finishes prefill, its computed state (the KV cache) is shipped to a decode machine, which generates the response token by token.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" layers</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That covers the efficiency techniques at each layer of an agentic AI application. The harness avoids resending what the server already has, the API avoids reprocessing what it has already processed, and inference avoids recomputing what it has already computed. To close, let’s look at the lessons from this work that apply beyond OpenAI.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>What to Learn from OpenAI’s Push for Efficiency and Lower Cost per Successful Task</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Zooming out, all these optimization techniques at different layers try to avoid paying for the same work twice. The harness sends only what is new and keeps prefixes stable so caches survive. The API tokenizes only the delta and hides unavoidable work inside windows that had to pass anyway. Inference routes conversations back to their cached state instead of recomputing it. These layers also feed each other. When the harness keeps the cache intact and the API improves the cache hit rate, the savings appear on the GPUs, which means lower costs for users. Beyond the techniques, here are a few lessons that the OpenAI engineers shared with us.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Keep the design simple.</span></strong><span> Prioritize simplicity over complexity. For example, use lexical search instead of embeddings for tool discovery, and one compaction path instead of a menu. An LLM is already quite intelligent, so adding more machinery in front of it often adds complexity without adding value. Build the simplest thing that could work, then scale it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Use the agent to optimize its own stack.</span></strong><span> Codex wrote much of the migration of the very API that serves Codex, turning years of rewrite work into months for a couple of engineers. The inference team uses it to analyze traces and prototype kernels. When agents write the code, you no longer need a language that is easy for humans to write, so you simply pick the most efficient one to run. Efficiency work is becoming a loop that accelerates itself.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><strong><span>Optimize end to end. </span></strong><span>The inference team told us that every time they picked one favorite technique to focus on, they regretted it. Focusing on one part of the stack made them underinvest in the others. No single optimization is a game changer on its own. The big wins come from chaining many small ones together. They also learned to test with the same traffic shapes that production actually serves, because a change that looks like a win offline can hurt in real traffic.</span></p></div></div><div This means no Thursday article this week, and no articles next week. I appreciate your understanding and support!</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Back to today’s deepdive, we cover:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Complex & long: Claude Managed Agents</span></strong><span>. One of the most complicated projects took the Claude Platform team six months to ship, and created a new primitive to use at the agent infra level. Infra projects still need re-architecting mid-way through and take time to get right.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Twelve-month project done in 11 days: Bun rewrite to Rust. </span></strong><span>Migrating a 500K+ line project to another language used to take a small team a year, making it impractical. With Fable and $165K of tokens, it recently took the creator of the project less than two weeks.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Changing engineering practices</span></strong><span>. Inside the AI lab with more than 3,500 employees, prototyping is more fluid, verification is more time-consuming than implementation, code review and testing are increasingly done by AI.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Team-level changes. </span></strong><span>Design is more ongoing and less upfront, teams work on more projects, a maximum of two engineers per project, and more.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Still the same: </span></strong><span>two-pizza teams, planning is important, PRDs are relevant in complex projects, context switching is a challenge, the ratio of time spent on coding vs testing not changing that much.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Changing the “standout” software engineer archetype? </span></strong><span>Deep understanding, including of a layer below what you work on, is valuable, along with the ability to coordinate work.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Will AI replace software engineering? </span></strong><span>The more hands-on software engineers get with AI at the lab, the less they fear their jobs are going away.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>The bottom of this article could be cut off in some email clients. </span><a does:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“We’re on the ‘token hot path.’ The prompt comes in, then we tokenize it. Then, things like safeguards and billing all happen within our layer.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>What the Claude team calls “Platform,” I think more of as “API.”</span></em><span> Claude Platform operates the API, and owns responsibilities an API would have. </span><em><span>Of course, the team does more than that, and Claude Managed Agents is one case we cover here.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The platform layer is being migrated from Python to Rust. </span></strong><span>Originally, this layer was written for Python for the “usual” reasons at AI companies: it’s a convenient language and AI researchers use Python already, which enables quick iteration. But Python is single-threaded, and at scale, when the API is under high load, it’s not as performant as Rust.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Harness infrastructure demand</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The project came together due to customers wanting their own “harness infrastructure”, says Katelyn:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“We started with a model where you get an API to define an agent, then you get an API to start a session with an agent. The reality of what the world wants and needs right now is people running their own infrastructure. So, we started to build a self-hosted sandbox.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But then, what we started to hear from lots of customers is that they’re trying to hack harnesses together, running their own “harness infrastructure,” and this gave us the idea for Claude Managed Agents.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>The largest part: planning</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this project, Katelyn said the single biggest matter was planning:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“There are products you can jump straight to prototyping, but then there are ones where you need to start by architecting it properly. For example, if we build a TypeScript CLI – which is pretty trivial for what needs to be built – we could go straight to prototyping. But with Claude Managed Agents, we needed to first figure out what we are doing.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Of course, we did some upfront prototyping for Managed Agents: hacking and spiking things. But prototyping itself was more about understanding the requirements.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Our planning process looked more like a typical pre-AI planning process. </span></strong><span>You know how every team has the project, where everyone comes up with some version of the same idea and people keep floating and circling it around until you finally do it? Managed Agents was this for our team. When we started the project, we had documents dating back up to two years about ideas and suggestions.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Post-planning, when the project officially kicked off, a PRD (product requirements document) was created:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“In the end, it was the Product Manager and the Tech Lead on our API Agents team who decided to pull the trigger and kick off this project. We’d get in a room, go through it, and get aligned. But it wasn’t just us: we’d have to align with teams around the business, other cloud providers, and other engineering teams. For example, we have a sandboxing team inside of the Platform org: and so this team was consulted on the design of Managed Agents, given this product would spawn a lot of sandboxes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Just like before, we had a PRD, it was a Google Doc. </span></strong><span>We used a Google Doc because we needed to coordinate all interested people. This has not gone away.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Similarly, my product counterpart and I run product reviews.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Some processes from before AI, like the PRD, are still useful in complex projects today, for getting large groups of people on the same page.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Build for an internal customer first</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With planning complete, the team decided to do a “spike” and stress-test the idea and architecture, by building the backend of Claude Code on the web. Remote execution of code with an agent harness was a similarly shaped problem to the one they wanted to solve for customers. The thinking was to start by solving it for the Claude Code team before tackling it in a more generic way for customers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Internal teams are more fluid than before AI. </span></strong><span>Katelyn:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Pre-AI, we might have hit the Claude Code team up with a bunch of big requirements documents, and they would have then hit us back with another set of documents. Now it was much easier: someone on our team built a few components, took it over to the Claude Code team, and they started to hack around it. We could figure out how this component plugs into this part of their product, and the other way around. It was just a faster and easier process, getting this first internal version of the product up and running.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Aligning with other teams on interfaces remains important, and it’s easier.</span><strong><span> </span></strong><span>Back in the day, you’d have to come with a fully spec’d interface to use. Now, we could do it a lot more fluidly: we could stand up a stub service that shadowed traffic to start with, and iron out the interfaces with the Claude Code team as we went. They did some hacking on it and gave feedback, we made changes while building out the service under the interface, then went back to make it work.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>They launched a service for Claude Code’s mobile app to spin up a sandbox, boot up Claude Code and run it. The service went to production and the Claude Platform team took the learnings.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Re-architecting midway through</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s likely a familiar scenario many engineers can relate to, that after planning a project and getting underway, you see that you’re going to need to change the architecture. It happened on this project, too.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The platform team ended up re-architecting Managed Agents based on learnings from the Claude Code “spike.” </span></strong><span>Re-architecting meant decoupling the “brain” of Claude and its harness from the “hands” (sandboxes & tools that perform actions) and the “session” (the log of events). Each became an interface that made few assumptions about each other.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 However, it’s not memory safe and memory issues </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c2617aca-9554-462b-9b7f-08206346f045?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>kept coming up</span></a><span>. Jarred thought that rewriting the project to an also-performant, memory-safe language like Rust could be an option – except that rewrites like this turned out as follies in the past. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f1f479bb-72c6-4b9b-b044-6b36b1b1b37e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Jarred</span></a><span> (emphasis mine:)</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Historically, rewrites are a terrible idea. Excluding comments, Bun is 535,496 lines of Zig. A rewrite in another language would take a small team of engineers a full year. It would mean freezing bugfixes, security fixes or feature development for that time. The least risky approach to getting something shippable would be a mechanical port from Zig to Rust, with the minimal number of behavioral changes, using the exact same test suite we already use for testing Bun.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Fortunately, Bun’s own test suite is written in TypeScript which means it doesn’t depend on the runtime’s programming language.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>A year of zero user-facing impact was not an option we could consider.</span></strong><span> So, enforcement through code style to fix stability issues was our best bet, and was our plan when we added Rust-inspired smart pointers to Bun’s codebase.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But honestly, I didn’t want to do it. Homegrown smart pointers offer worse ergonomics than Rust, with none of the guarantees.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But then, Jarred asked if AI could do the heavy lifting and wondered how much the migration could be sped up. </span><strong><span>In the end, he completed the rewrite from start to merge in 11 days, using 64 parallel agents and $165,000 in tokens at API price. </span></strong><span>Here’s Jarred on how his AI-heavy rewrite compared:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“By hand, I think this would’ve taken three engineers with full context on the codebase about a year, during which time we wouldn’t be able to improve Node.js compatibility, fix bugs, fix security issues or implement new features. We never would’ve done that. The realistic alternative was to do nothing and keep fixing the bugs at the top of this post forever.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There was a lot more to the project than typing out the “...make zero mistakes” prompt:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Jarred made a detailed plan and style guide on how to migrate</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>He set up the project so agents would not use Git worktrees which he found slow, but worked on different files in the same codebase</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>He created an orchestration system where each AI agent came up with suggestions of what to change, but did not make a change to the file to avoid conflicts; an orchestrator AI agent created the commits</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The most time and tokens went on fixing the compile bugs, tests, and verifying that things worked</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Bun itself has a very robust test harness: when all tests pass, it’s a high-confidence signal that the rewrite works</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Crucially, Jarred is </span><em><span>the</span></em><span> ultimate domain expert in Bun: he created the project and knows the codebase better than anyone</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Changing engineering practices</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So, what has changed in how teams build software at Anthropic, compared to the pre-AI days? That’s the question of this article, and it seems that many things are different. Let’s go through it:</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>AI lab-specific practices</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Some things as normal as breathing at AI labs like Anthropic stand out as different with an outside perspective:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Everyone runs multiple AI agents all the time. </span></strong><span>Running 3-10 parallel agents is a given. Folks I talked with had their agents running in the background or cloud.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>No token budget, usage not tracked. </span></strong><span>One major difference between AI labs and everyone else is that there </span><em><span>really</span></em><span> is no token limit or token leaderboards that promote tokenmaxxing; people already use agents all the time.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Very high autonomy. </span></strong><span>Work is becoming more structured inside AI labs, but there’s still massive autonomy compared to Big Tech and most startups. When everyone has unlimited tokens, it’s pretty easy to prototype any idea.</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Prototyping and “spiking” is far more fluid</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It was several times faster to prototype early approaches for Claude Managed Agents. optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Most tokens no longer spent on implementation</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Thariq:</span></strong></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“We see that few tokens are spent on actual implementation. Most are spent on discovery of unknowns, prototyping, mocking, and then in verification and testing.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Jarred’s Bun rewrite echoes this: he spent more tokens on fixing up the implementation and verifying that it worked than on the implementation itself!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Code review and more testing by AI</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Jarred:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Critiquing the code and testing it with agents is a new approach we do a lot more of</span><strong><span>.</span></strong><span> I think a lot about trust when you merge a lot of code. How do you merge 100+ PRs a day, and make sure the code works? At this pace, you need to trust the code without the ability to read it all yourself. And I think it’s a few things:</span></p><ul style="margin-left: 20px;margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Code review</span></strong><span>: it needs to be really good and automated. I’m clearly tooting our own horn here, but I find Claude’s code review to be really good. Claude’s code review catches bugs that would take me an hour of closely reading the code to figure out. The caveat is that it’s expensive!</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Security scanning</span></strong><span>: for this Rust rewrite we did 11 runs of the Claude Security Scanner.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Fuzz testing</span></strong><span>: we’ve also been doing different types of fuzzing (</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f069bd2f-e0aa-40a4-9a1e-80f77a6d9efd?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>fuzz testing</span></a><span>), where we had Claude write a fuzzer for things like parser fuzzing.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Running out-of-process testing, where it happens in a different process/session from coding, is one way to build trust in the code. I expect more of this.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>New pattern: fanning out work to AI</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Jarred described a new way he works:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“A new approach I’m using is fanning out a lot of the work to many Claudes at the same time. I did this with the Bun rewrite, but I use it for other work. This approach works very well for me, and I feel it’s pretty underused.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Time-saving automations powered by agents more widespread</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Jarred listed several time-saving automations set up by the Bun team to run an active open-source project with a small team, while the team works on Claude Code:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Every time someone files an issue, Claude runs to try and reproduce the issue. If it succeeds, it starts another container, which then tries to fix the issue and submit a PR.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The agent tasked with submitting a PR has to write a test that fails in the system version (the one without the patch) of Bun, and passes in the debug build with the patch, before it is allowed to submit a PR</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>There are other automations, like if there is no test, the PR is auto-rejected; all linters are run: Claude Code review is run, CodeRabbit’s code review is run, and the agents go back and forth on the GitHub pull request</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Auto-merge of pull requests: coming soon?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Pull requests are merged manually when all quality gates pass, but this could become automatic at some point. Once all the above checks pass, all (AI) code review comments are addressed, tests are added to new code, etc. As an interesting aside, a lot of GitHub activity is Claude talking to Claude!</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" Jarred told me:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Today, a person presses ‘merge’ but within a few months, I expect:</span></p></blockquote><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Automated reviewer LGTMs</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>→ another Claude with a fresh context window judges if it’s simple and low blast-radius</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>→ if it is: auto-merge!”</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Test assumptions with each model generation</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Inside Anthropic, the team keeps testing their priors. Thariq gave an interesting example:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The thing with agents is that you have to revisit any assumptions you have made because it can change with a new model generation. For that reason, we deleted 80% of the Claude Code system prompt recently because the model has gotten smarter.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Using HTML is another assumption we needed to re-examine.</span></strong><span> HTML is one of those things which Claude is a lot smarter at than many of us expected. I’ve started preferring HTML as an output format over Markdown, and see this being used by others on the Claude Code team.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>HTML can convey much richer information compared to markdown, HTML documents are easier to read and share.”</span></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>4. Team-level changes</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At Anthropic, there are also changes in how engineering teams operate, compared to pre-AI.</span></p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Design is less upfront & more continuous on product teams</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Katelyn:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“As an engineer, you used to be able to say, “here’s a perfect, beautiful design.” </span><strong><span>In some teams inside the Anthropic org, upfront planning is gone.</span></strong><span> There are parts of the Anthropic org where people have said things like “we don’t write PRDs” or “we don’t write technical design documents anymore.” Those teams go straight to prototypes.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s worth bearing in mind the differences between platform and product teams, and the maturity of products. The more platform-like and mature a product is, the more that the value of upfront planning rises.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Silos no longer a worry</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Katelyn confirmed that while the typical size of the platform teams has not changed much – they’re still 6-8 people – but now, they take on far more projects than in the past.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Pre-AI, if a team worked on more than one project at a time, members would complain about feeling siloed: cut off from what peers on the team were doing. But now, it’s common to find 3-8 parallel projects on a 6–8-person team.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Two engineers max on individual projects</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Katelyn:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“On an individual project, you often cannot have more than two people working on it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>This is because each engineer is already running several agents</span></strong><span>. And so as an engineer, you’re already fighting against your agents, which are stepping on each other’s toes on implementation. And in this setup, you just cannot have that many humans, who also come with all their agents! This is especially true when the human is doing more of the actual design of the system.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Katelyn has a point: before AI, it was also a recipe for disaster to have several tech leads on the same project!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Internal teams iterate faster</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Pre-AI, teams went through the back-and-forth of iterating on an implementation using design documents. Now, for the Claude Managed Agents project, it took the form of the Claude Code team hacking around the implementation. Katelyn told me the whole process felt faster and easier than before AI tools.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>5. Still the same</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Here’s what I gathered from my four conversations with Anthropic insiders about what’s not changed in software engineering much since AI came along.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Two-pizza teams</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On the Platform side, there are 6–8-person teams as there were before AI in platform organizations. Katelyn on why this hasn’t changed:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I still have teams whose job it is to own a piece of software, iterate on it, own oncall, and so on. While each of these humans are supercharged by AI, the size and shape of the team is still similar. We still have two-pizza teams.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Everybody on the team needs to have a deep understanding of the system. </span></strong><span> They need to understand where it’s going, then orchestrate their Claudes to build in that direction. But people still need to internalize how their system works. So, the system they work on cannot become so big that someone doesn’t understand it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But then, you also need enough people so that when someone is oncall, another is on vacation, and someone is sick, you still have redundancy and the team can continue to make progress.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>One thing I’ve heard from some people is “we have two humans and a bunch of agents.” </span></strong><span>I reply that this isn’t where we’re at: we still have teams with 6-8 people on average.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Planning still important</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Both Katelyn and Jarred mentioned the importance of planning, but with different focuses:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For Managed Agents, the planning process was the most similar to how it was pre-AI, due to the complexity:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Infrastructure complexity: the platform itself is complex, with lots of parts that needed consideration</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The number of people/teams involved: a lot of people and groups needed to be aligned: not just the Platform team, but other teams at Anthropic, and working with three different cloud providers.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>This takes time to get it right!</span></p></li></ul></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>For the Bun rewrite, Jarred started by spending three hours talking to Claude about how to map patterns from their Zig codebase closely to Rust</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For complex projects with many people or systems, planning still matters at Anthropic. Even for kicking off a “simpler” project like a migration, a few hours of intense preparation and planning is seen as worthwhile.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Also, let’s not forget that in the Bun rewrite, the planning part was greatly shortened by Jarred being the creator and de facto domain expert. Also, there were no other engineers, which further shortened the process.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>PRDs in some teams</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>PRDs are for when lots of people need to be coordinated, and the Claude Managed Agents project is a good case. PRDs inside Anthropic are Google Docs because the point of this document is for it to be debated, and for agreement reached about a complex project’s high-level goals and design approach.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Platform/product split & prototype/mature product split</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There’s a big difference between building a product and building a system, as with upfront design being far more of a thing with systems than it ever is with products.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For products, there is maturity to consider. For example, Claude Code during infancy was more of a prototype. It then found product-market fit, and today it’s a mature product with millions of customers. Prototyping can be a great way to get a product off the ground. But the more mature it becomes, the more planning might be needed for things like a new feature that needs to integrate nicely with other parts of the product, or product-wide changes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It was the same pre-AI; we covered how Uber introduced platform and product teams in 2014 in </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6a1c3c48-9b31-4648-a7f9-ca0a5d1abaf2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>The platform/program split at Uber</span></a><span>, </span><em><span>the first-ever Pragmatic Engineer article</span></em><span>.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Platform work challenging as ever</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Katelyn, again:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“There’s a bit of a different working culture between application development and platform development. For example, when we’re building new things into the platform, we deploy on all three clouds (AWS, GCP, Azure), and deploy in several regions. We’ll eventually start deploying internationally. It makes for a lot of complexity.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>We have specialized teams within the org and a specialist team in each layer.</span></strong><span> We have abstraction layers in place, so most people don’t have to think about the physical infrastructure. But even so, within my org, I have a team who understand what queue implementations on each of the different clouds look like. In some cases, we’re running bare metal, and in other cases we’re running managed services. We always have a team that understands every part of a layer, and then other teams don’t need to become so specialist in a given layer.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Context switching still hard</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I asked if it’s now easier to ask an engineer on another team for help with your own work. I figured it should be when everyone uses AI, as it makes getting back in “the zone” easy after returning to your work from lending a hand. Katelyn didn’t see it like that:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Context switching, on one end, is easier, but it’s still very hard. In the past, it was a pretty big ask to go to an engineer doing deep work, to ask them to stop something to help you with feedback, or do some of your work. With AI, context switching is easier, but deep work has not gone away.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Agreement on interfaces still matters in cross-team engineering work</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Reflecting on Claude Managed Agents, Katelyn told me it’s important to define the interfaces between the Platform team building Managed Agents and the Claude Code team using it, as per pre-AI. The difference is that it’s a bit easier to iterate with AI:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“</span></strong><span>Back in the day, you’d have to come with a fully spec’d interface you wanted to use with the team you’re integrating with (for us, Claude Code). Now, we can do it a lot more fluidly: we could stand up a stub service that shadowed traffic to start with, and iron out the interfaces with the Claude Code team as we went. They did some hacking on it, gave feedback, we made changes to it – we were building out the service under the interface – to make it work.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Coding/testing time split hasn’t changed</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Time spent coding vs on testing hasn’t changed all that much from before AI,</span><strong><span> </span></strong><span>according to Jarred:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The AI writes pretty much all the code, but we have the AI write pretty much all the tests as well. Before AI, for production-ready software, we spent about the same time writing tests as we did on writing code. This is still the case with AI. You need to have a way to trust your code, and tests are probably the best way to.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What happens to the time created by not spending it on writing code and tests? Jarred says he doesn’t have more free time these days:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I now spend more time on making sure everything works and on doing a lot more stuff than before. There’s so much stuff in Bun that we would not have shipped [without time savings from AI]. For example, we have a Markdown parser and a YAML parser on Bun. I used to have a list of everything I’d like to do in Bun, and it’s pretty much all there!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The bottleneck used to be me or someone else spending a bunch of time writing code, then spending just as much time figuring out how to test it all and what test suite to build. But now, we can just mention Claude in Slack (using Claude Tag), it runs and gives us a PR to start with.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Learn something new to make something great</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Thariq Shihipar is responsible for much of the educational content on Claude Code. He’s a software engineer who tinkers a lot and shares what he learned; for example, how he got </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/82aebf22-5a7f-45a6-bebc-8dadb6e2ab23?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Fable to edit a launch video.</span></a><span> He also works with the Claude Code team and engineers outside Anthropic.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static"
