style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One thing Thariq doesn’t see changing in engineering is that it takes special effort to make something truly great. As he told me:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“</span><strong><span>When you’re looking at how to make something great, you usually need to learn something new.</span></strong><span> Say that you want to make a video game. People love vibe coding video games, but there’s so much to learn to make a really good game!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, if you’re making a flying game controlling a plane, there’s so much depth to how the plane reacts to the left and right movement. If you know about the domain, then Claude can work with you on it. But in my observation, you need to expand your own knowledge to be able to work efficiently with it to get to an end result that feels “great.”</span></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>6. Changing the “standout” software engineer archetype?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I asked both Katelyn and Jarred if and how the “standout” software engineer archetype has altered with the adoption of AI tools, and which traits make for a solid engineer, in their view.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Understand, understand, understand</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Jarred:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“It’s still really important to understand how everything works, end to end. Also, it’s important to not trust that because something was assumed to be true, that it still is true.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>A lot of programming is still like poking around and seeing what happens. </span></strong><span>So, have the mental model in your head and stay in charge. As a person, I am still deciding what to merge, and what I should work on. I’m still very nitpicky about </span><em><span>exactly</span></em><span> the way it should be done, and this comes from understanding. I think you can also just use AI to help you understand faster.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Katelyn said similar:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“Understanding is table stakes for solid engineers.</span></strong><span> Make sure you understand not just what the LLM does, but also a layer underneath it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The problem with models is the context window is finite. Our research team is working extremely hard so the model can feel like it has almost infinite context and that it will make the right decisions and store them away in memory, then pull it back in, and keep the  context window as clean as it can. But, at the end of the day, the model’s context window is finite and nowhere close to what a human brain can store – so keep investing in developing your own mind while you work with agents. Understanding and learning with the model is a great way.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Katelyn stressed that as an engineer, it’s important to understand not just the current layer, but also the one below it. For example, if building a product that uses queues, understand the queue primitive or implementation you’re using.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Coordination skill also table stakes</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Katelyn:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Coordination and alignment remain very important skills for engineers. Even if it gets easier to coordinate groups of people with AI tools, it’s not going away!”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I will add my own observation: every engineer I’ve met at Anthropic was a good communicator and articulate in expressing their ideas. I suspect the company would not hire folks who lack fluency in this and debating ideas.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Engineers designing software</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Katelyn:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Engineers are the ones doing the design, and it will probably stay like this for some time. Even as the models get better at technical design and systems design, I cannot see the model replacing my engineers on large-scale distributed systems design.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Steering the model in the right direction is very important. </span></strong><span>One more reason for understanding what the model does – and the layer below it – is that the model will get things wrong, inevitably. When it does, you want to steer the model to get it right.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Being “in the zone” has changed</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Jarred was a standout programmer pre-AI, and has spent a lot of his time “locked in” on writing code. Now that AI writes most of his code, I asked if he still gets “in the zone.” He told me:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“Being in the zone” as a developer is definitely different now. </span></strong><span>I still do things in serial order, sometimes. Not writing the code, but when you’re doing one project, there’s a lot going on and you see it coming together, step by step. As long as the feedback loops are quick enough, I find myself in a kind of “zone.” It’s admittedly different from the “coding” zone, but it’s really fun.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Another thing I like is that I can be away from my computer, and things are still happening. For example, I can be on a run and just check how the agent running in the background is doing.</span></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>7. Will AI replace software engineering?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In February 2025, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dbbce8b7-7147-4e4e-9254-5ab1855d50f1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>made an eye-catching prediction</span></a><span>, saying: “coding is going away first, then all of software engineering”. His comment:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I think coding is going away first, done by the AI models first. And the broader task of software engineering will take longer. Doing that end-to-end [AI replacing software engineering] is going to happen as well.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But the elements of design, or making something that is useful to the user, or managing teams of AI models: those things may still be present. Even if you’re doing 5% of a task, that 5% gets super amplified”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I asked Katelyn, Jarred, and David Hershey for their takes: do they see software engineering “going away” and being “solved” by Claude? </span><strong><span>Interestingly, people who build software day-to-day are not worried about models taking over software engineering. </span></strong><span>Katelyn and Jarred are confident they have lots of work to do, and feel busier with software engineering than before!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>They do lots of planning, coordination, verification, coming up with more effective ways to manage agents, and building novel software.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>David Hershey, who focuses heavily on customers, reckons the models will eventually take over software engineering:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I have a very hard time believing that the models will eventually not take over this thing that we call software engineering. It’s going to get better than us at nearly all of it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The model can already listen to customer feedback, and write the software to solve problems customers have. It’s hard to point to something it cannot do.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I watched models become better software engineers than me, and I have a software engineering degree. I don’t claim to be a great software engineer, but I don’t see why it would stop at my level and not keep outdoing most software engineers.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Based on my small sample size, it seems that the more hands-on someone is in software engineering, the less they believe the models will take their jobs. Both Katelyn and Jarred stressed the importance of understanding everything about your system, how it works, and to keep going ever deeper in understanding it – especially with the help of AI!</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Takeaways</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It was an interesting day at Anthropic, with much food for thought afterwards about the ways that software engineering has changed and where it might be headed next. </span><em><span>Thanks very much to everyone there for welcoming me and sharing their time.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>I suspect the way software engineering is done inside Anthropic will be how many “AI-native” startups will operate soon </span></strong><span>– if not already. Specifically:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Projects done by a maximum of two engineers, and a bunch of AI agents</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Design is more ongoing and less upfront</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A lot more prototyping, with more detailed planning only for complex projects</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>… but things still take time, even with faster coding! AI has not magically solved how to build quality software that’s complex and does something customers want.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The software engineering bar has shifted upward at Anthropic. </span></strong><span>Every engineer I talked with there is “standout” in more than one dimension:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Solid engineers pre-AI: these folks were very good engineers before the AI wave</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Push themselves every day: they experiment with new approaches with (or without!) AI, change workflows, and keep learning how to best employ the latest models in their work</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Collaboration and coordination are key: they self-manage themselves, stakeholders, and teams when needed</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>High-profile labs in leading positions like Anthropic get to hire the “best of the best” software engineers, and one question is what this means for companies without the brand recognition and funding of an Anthropic. Perhaps this kind of setup only works when you can hire such standout engineers, and for companies without the ability to attract such standout folks, attempting to copy what Anthropic does could well result in disappointment, without similarly motivated and capable staff.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Today, Anthropic generates five times more revenue per employee than Big Tech.</span></strong><span> Anthropic is made up of somewhat over 3,500 people, and annual revenue run-rate </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a2c9d953-e36d-436a-891e-a4d51e242d37?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>crossed</span></a><span> $47 billion this May. That’s roughly $13.5M in revenue per employee: at Meta it’s $2.7M/employee, Apple $2.6M, and at Google $2.2M. NVIDIA is the only major company that comes close with $6M/employee.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure Such revenue also allows them to keep hiring top talent with the biggest comp packages on the market.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We should state the obvious, that Anthropic is in the business of selling AI models, so using AI heavily is obvious for them. But they also support a very large number of customers and enterprises with a surprisingly small team, and using AI more than most companies is clearly one way to operate with so many fewer employees.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Teams are remarkably unchanged, though. </span></strong><span>One familiar part of how Anthropic works is that a “team” is still a core building block of the engineering organization, and it’s made up of 6-8 engineers as it was before AI.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The replacement of the team with two people and dozens of agents is not happening at Anthropic because it would not promote sustainable operations. As Katelyn said about the team size:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“One thing I’ve heard from some people is ‘we have two humans and a bunch of agents.’ I reply that this isn’t where we’re at: we still have teams with 6-8 people on average.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>I hope you found this look into how Anthropic works interesting. In a future article, I’ll share details from inside OpenAI following a visit to their offices, and we’ll have the chance to compare the two.</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>This post is only for paying subscribers of </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIwODg0ODk0MCwicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6MTkzMDQzMTQ4LCJpYXQiOjE3ODUyNTQxMTIsImV4cCI6MjEwMDgzMDExMiwiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.htbomr3SZp3auYhYhbphFOvnGxHWVe7wdnhJngfkr1s?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em>. You call the real provider API with a fresh token, every time.</span><br></p><p class="button-wrapper" data-attrs="{"url":"https://go.bytebytego.com/WorkOS_072826CTA","text":"Connect to 100+ providers →","action":null,"class":null}" data-component-name="ButtonCreateButton" style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: center;cursor: pointer;border-radius: 4px;"><a class="button primary" href="https://substack.com/redirect/12fb6dbc-9ebb-45aa-87fc-190b1d757715?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="font-family: system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';display: inline-block;box-sizing: border-box;cursor: pointer;border: none;border-radius: 8px;font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 600;text-align: center;margin: 0;opacity: 1;outline: none;white-space: nowrap;color: #ffffff !important;text-decoration: none !important;background-color: #7756e3;padding: 12px 20px;height: auto;"><span style="color: #ffffff;text-decoration: none;">Connect to 100+ providers →</span></a></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Over the last few years, three of the biggest food delivery companies rebuilt their search systems around LLMs. DoorDash, Instacart, and Uber Eats were solving the same problem of trying to understand a user’s intent when they type something in search. They were also accessing more or less the same research base. And yet, the architectures they shipped look quite different from each other.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That divergence is one of the most interesting aspects of modern development using LLMs. Once we understand why each company landed where it did, we will have a mental model for thinking about how AI can be integrated into any production system.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Adding an LLM to an existing stack comes down to one question: how deeply should the LLM reach into the runtime?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Ultimately, DoorDash, Instacart, and Uber Eats each answered that question differently, and the specific LLM each chose was secondary. The specific model each company picked was secondary. The infrastructure they already had in place is what determined the answer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we will walk through their differing solutions and try to make sense of their choices and understand the pattern behind them.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References are present at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>The Problem</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Type “something healthy for a rainy evening” into a food delivery app and watch what comes back. The result we get today is somewhere between useful and impressive. The same query five years ago might have returned a random jumble of items, because keyword search treats the words as a bag of tokens rather than as an intent, and the query offers little for keyword matching.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This pattern repeats across several common failure modes in food search. For example:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Synonyms:</span></strong><span> “Soda” and “soft drink” describe the same product, but a keyword engine treats them as different tokens.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Typos:</span></strong><span> “Mozzarela” should retrieve mozzarella results, but the spelling mismatch breaks the lookup.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Shorthand:</span></strong><span> “Gf pizza” meaning gluten-free pizza requires the system to recognize an abbreviation as a synonym for the full phrase.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Language mix:</span></strong><span> The Spanish word “pan” means bread, while the English word “pan” means a cooking vessel, so a bilingual search bar has to disambiguate.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Word-sense ambiguity:</span></strong><span> “Apple” the fruit and “Apple” the company share the same spelling but mean different things, and the right answer depends on context.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each one is a potential moment where the user’s intent and the catalog’s words fail to line up.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>DoorDash</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>DoorDash already had a knowledge graph for items and restaurants when LLMs became viable for production. The graph held structured attributes for every item, including dish type, dietary preference, cuisine, brand, and flavor.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Their approach was to use LLMs to enrich this graph offline by extracting attributes from SKU data, and to use LLMs at runtime only for parsing queries into chunks that could link back to the graph. Retrieval itself stayed keyword and graph-driven.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Consider the query “small no-milk vanilla ice cream.” The LLM segments it into three chunks.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>“small” is a quantity attribute.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>“no-milk” is a dietary preference attribute that maps to the canonical label “dairy-free.”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>“vanilla ice cream” splits further into a dish type (”ice cream”) and a flavor (”vanilla”).</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each chunk is then linked to a specific field in the knowledge graph. The dietary preference becomes a hard filter, so only dairy-free items get retrieved. The flavor becomes a soft preference for ranking. The dish type narrows the candidate pool.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div DoorDash’s approach is how they constrain the LLM’s outputs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>They use retrieval-augmented generation as a guardrail rather than as a generator. For each query segment, an approximate nearest neighbor lookup retrieves the top 100 closest taxonomy concepts from the existing graph. The LLM is then prompted to pick from that list rather than invent labels. This is a clever inversion of the usual RAG pattern, where RAG typically injects context into a generator. Here, RAG defines the entire output space, so the system only ever produces concepts that the rest of the design already knows how to handle.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The measured impact is a roughly 30% lift in the trigger rate for popular dish carousels, all delivered through an architecture whose runtime stays mostly classical.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The takeaway is that DoorDash’s LLM lives mostly offline, mostly in batch, working on the periphery of the runtime.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Instacart</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When Instacart’s engineers first investigated an off-the-shelf LLM to categorize the search query “protein,” the model returned chicken, tofu, beef, and other high-protein foods.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The answer is reasonable by any reading of the English language. The problem is that Instacart’s actual users, when they type “protein,” are looking for protein bars and protein powders. The model’s general world knowledge and the company’s specific user behavior were pulling in different directions, and this small failure points at the central problem Instacart had to solve.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The system they were replacing was complex.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Query category classification ran on a FastText model, query rewrites came from a separate engine that mined session behavior, and spell correction, query tagging, and aisle classification each ran as a separate model with its own data pipeline and serving infrastructure. The maintenance burden was substantial, and tail queries still suffered because each model needed its own labeled data, and labels for rare queries are scarce by definition.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Instacart’s strategy is layered across three approaches:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Context engineering:</span></strong><span> Retrieval-augmented generation pulls Instacart-specific context (top-converted categories, historical conversion data, catalog details) into the prompt before the LLM sees a query.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Post-processing guardrails:</span></strong><span> Semantic similarity filters drop LLM outputs that drift away from the original query.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Fine-tuning:</span></strong><span> For the most advanced tasks, the team fine-tunes Llama-3-8B on Instacart’s proprietary data, so domain knowledge gets baked directly into the model weights.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The serving architecture splits along the head-versus-tail distribution.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Head queries hit an offline RAG-and-cache pipeline that is latency-tolerant and deeply context-engineered, while tail queries hit a real-time fine-tuned Llama-3-8B model that keeps latency under 300ms through adapter merging, H100 GPUs, and autoscaling.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The cache serves queries the company has seen before, while the real-time fine-tuned model serves everything else, which is where the cold-start tail lives. This split is exactly the kind of decision the head-versus-tail traffic distribution encourages, since pre-computing only pays off for queries that repeat.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>After this solution, query rewrite coverage jumped from 50% to over 95%, with 90%+ precision across substitutes, broader rewrites, and synonyms. The real-time fine-tuned model improved search quality for the bottom 2% of queries (the cold-start tail), cutting scroll depth by 6% and complaints about poor tail-query results by half.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The takeaway is that Instacart’s LLMs live at the query understanding layer, with some offline-cached and some online and fine-tuned, while retrieval and ranking downstream are still done by traditional machine learning and information retrieval systems. The LLM brain is doing the upstream interpretation, while the classical approach is doing the downstream serving.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Uber Eats</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Uber Eats faced the same problem the others did, plus a complication. They run across multiple verticals, including restaurants, grocery, and retail, across multiple markets, and across a long list of languages.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Their previous setup was fragmented, with separate BERT-based embedding models per vertical, lexical search in places, and the operational overhead of maintaining all of these in parallel. The goal was a single retrieval system that handled every vertical, every market, and every language with one consistent embedding space.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The architecture they decided on is a classic two-tower setup, where a query encoder and a document encoder each produce vectors in a shared space, and matching is done by similarity in that space.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The twist is in what sits inside each tower, because both towers use a fine-tuned Qwen LLM as their backbone embedding layer. The query tower runs online, embedding each incoming query in real time, while the document tower runs offline and pre-embeds billions of documents into an HNSW vector index (a graph-based structure built for fast similarity search at scale). This split is what makes the system economically possible, since running a heavyweight LLM on every document at query time would be prohibitive, while pre-computing once and looking up at retrieval time is tractable.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The fine-tuning matters as much as the architecture choice.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Out of the box, Qwen brings world knowledge and cross-lingual capability, which is what handles the Spanish “pan” problem mentioned earlier. Fine-tuning on Uber’s proprietary query-document interactions teaches the embedding space what Uber Eats users actually care about, and this is what gives the system its domain alignment. The base model contributes general semantics, and the fine-tuning adds the specific rules of Uber Eats.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What makes the system viable at scale is a stack of optimizations:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Matryoshka Representation Learning trains a single model whose embedding can be truncated to different lengths, and Uber serves at 256 dimensions in production with under 0.3% recall loss compared to the full 1,536.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Scalar quantization (int7 instead of float32) cuts latency in half again.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Pre-filters on hexagon, city, and fulfillment type shrink the candidate set before the ANN search even runs.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The numbers tell the cost story. Tuning the ANN parameter k dropped latency by 34% and CPU by 17% with negligible recall impact, quantization halved latency at recall above 0.95, and MRL cut storage by nearly 50%. Together, these are the engineering choices that let a fine-tuned LLM serve as the retrieval substrate of a production search system at Uber Eats’ scale.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The takeaway is that Uber Eats’ LLM is the embedding model itself, since every query and every document gets an LLM-derived vector, and retrieval at every level depends on LLM-produced representations.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Integration Depth</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If we line up the three companies on a single axis labeled “how deeply does the LLM sit in the runtime,” the pattern provides some insight.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>DoorDash sits on the left, with the LLM enriching the catalog offline and parsing queries with constrained outputs while the runtime stays mostly classical.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Instacart sits in the middle, with LLMs handling query understanding through offline RAG for the head queries and a fine-tuned Llama-3-8B for the tail, while retrieval downstream is still traditional.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Uber Eats sits on the right, with a fine-tuned Qwen as the embedding backbone running for every query and pre-baked into every document vector.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: position on the spectrum was largely determined by the infrastructure it already had.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>DoorDash already had a knowledge graph that classical retrieval could exploit, so the cheapest gain came from making the graph richer and teaching queries how to talk to it.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Instacart had specialized query-understanding models that were hard to maintain, so the biggest win came from consolidation under a unified LLM strategy.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Uber Eats already had two-tower embedding infrastructure running per vertical, so the natural next step was swapping in a fine-tuned LLM as the shared backbone, allowing one model to handle every vertical and every language.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The lesson would be that before asking which LLM to use for some task, the better question is where in an existing stack an LLM would actually help.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Three of the largest food delivery companies rebuilt search around LLMs in the same window of time, with overlapping research literature and similar production constraints, and they arrived at three completely distinct architectures.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The reason food search was a good place to investigate this is that it breaks classical keyword retrieval in many ways simultaneously. Subjective queries (something healthy for a rainy evening), long-tail traffic, multilingual catalogs, and compound constraints all sit in the same search bar.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The three approaches each represent a different setting:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>DoorDash uses LLMs offline to enrich a knowledge graph, while classical retrieval still drives the runtime.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Instacart uses LLMs at the query understanding layer, with fine-tuned smaller models handling tail queries in the hot path.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Uber Eats fine-tuned a Qwen LLM into the embedding backbone of two-tower retrieval, so every query and every document gets an LLM-derived vector.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each company’s position on this spectrum traces back to the infrastructure it already had, which is why the depth-of-integration question matters more than the model choice.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Three universal tradeoffs survived every architecture.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Hybrid systems are the default everywhere. Classical retrieval, knowledge graphs, and ANN indexes still do most of the work.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>World knowledge from a pre-trained model is just a head start. Domain context still has to be injected somewhere, through RAG, fine-tuning, or both.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Guardrails are an important part of every production LLM system. Constrained vocabularies, similarity filters, and taxonomy enforcement quietly determine whether outputs stay aligned with the catalog.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: item.description: Why DoorDash, Instacart, and Uber Eats Integrated LLMs Into Search Three Different Ways

item.title: Mission To Metrics
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Mission To Metrics

Annie Zhou

“Mission to Metrics is a written cascade, running from why the org exists down to the numbers that measure whether it’s getting there. Every team’s plan is a more detailed version of one slice of the layer above. Every metric traces back to the mission. Once it’s written, anyone in the org can read the page and understand how their work connects to the company mission.”

#Leadership Management Metrics
item.description: Mission To Metrics

item.title: The Vital Few
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Vital Few

Mike Fisher

“Stewardship is the actual work. It means giving your strongest people air cover, not just assignments. It means defending their focus from the steady drizzle of interruptions that drifts toward competence. It means offering them growth rather than merely more volume, and fighting the reflex to drop the next critical thing on the proven desk simply because it is proven.”

#Leadership Management Retention
item.description: The Vital Few

item.title: Make No Assumptions
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Make No Assumptions

Will Larson

“When that architect leaves, they are replaced by someone who aspires to operate in the same code layer, but simply cannot because they lack enough context to do so. As a result, that new replacement creates a new code layer, despite not intending to. If the team runs through a handful of folks as the new team leads struggle, it’s easy to end up with a complex code horizon very quickly.”

#Leadership AI CodeReview
item.description: Make No Assumptions

item.title: The State Of AI Impact In Engineering: Q2 2026
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The State Of AI Impact In Engineering: Q2 2026

Justin Reock

“Engineering leaders are now under immense pressure to justify exponentially-increasing AI budgets. The data from our Q2 report reveals that while AI is delivering objective gains in velocity, those gains are highly uneven.”

#Survey AI IndustryTrends
item.description: The State Of AI Impact In Engineering: Q2 2026

item.title: Building Ask DoorDash: A Platform For Building and Evolving Agents
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Building Ask DoorDash: A Platform For Building and Evolving Agents

“We built Ask DoorDash on a common platform that lets domain teams build and evolve their agents without rebuilding the systems beneath them. We judged the platform by two practical outcomes: how quickly teams could add features and domains, and how quickly they could evaluate and release improvements to cost, quality, and latency.”

#Architecture PlatformEng Agents
item.description: Building Ask DoorDash: A Platform For Building and Evolving Agents

item.title: The New Rules Of Context Engineering For Claude 5 Models
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The New Rules Of Context Engineering For Claude 5 Models

Thariq Shihipar

“Here’s what we’ve learned about prompting this new class of models, and how you can utilize it to update your context engineering. We’ve put these best practices in claude doctor, use the command /doctor in Claude Code to rightsize your skills, and CLAUDE.md files.”

#Guide AI
item.description: The New Rules Of Context Engineering For Claude 5 Models

item.title: The Git History Command Deserves More Attention
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Git History Command Deserves More Attention

Lalit Maganti

"Working with lots of changes in parallel on git can be painful. You end up juggling branches and commits, and running scary rebase -i commands that can leave your tree in a half-broken state if you so much as sneeze.”

#Git
item.description: The Git History Command Deserves More Attention

Physical AI</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Language models are great at predicting the next token, but they do not understand the physical world. They cannot tell you how a shirt sleeve folds, or what a glass of water looks like the moment it tips over. A robot or a self-driving car needs that kind of understanding, but it cannot get it from text.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That is what a world model provides. Instead of predicting the next word, it understands the world and can predict the next state given the current state of the world and an action. It can generate realistic, physically plausible video, reason about motion and cause and effect, and produce the action data a robot needs to learn.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>World models are extremely useful because you can use them to create training data for situations that are slow, expensive, or dangerous to capture in the real world.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table Alpamayo is an open model family for reasoning-based self-driving. Like GR00T, it uses Cosmos as its reasoning backbone, so the same physical-AI foundation that powers robots also lets a car work through road situations it was never trained on. It also exposes the chain of cause and effect behind each decision, which developers can inspect and build on. BioNeMo brings open models to biology and drug discovery, and the BioNeMo Agent Toolkit lets developers build autonomous agents for life sciences work. Ising gives quantum computer builders, operators, and developers the AI tools needed to scale devices to fault tolerance. Earth-2 is a family of open models, libraries, and frameworks that makes professional-grade weather and climate AI available to anyone. On top of these, NVIDIA offers open models for production use: safety models that filter unsafe content, speech models for voice, and vision models for images.</span></p><div style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Taken together, this powerful ecosystem changes how the community can advance and build. The rest of the article looks at how NVIDIA builds these models, how the team is able to move fast, and what they have learned.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>How the Models Are Built to Be Frontier and Fast</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It is often a challenge to build a model that is both fast and capable. Capable models are usually larger, which makes them slower to train and to answer questions. NVIDIA’s answer is to chase the frontier and speed at the same time. Bryan put it this way: “the fastest model is the smartest model.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>While this may sound like a slogan, it has a real insight. A faster model can be trained on more data in the same amount of time. It can be post-trained across more environments. Once deployed, it can think for longer on a hard problem at the same cost. So speed translates into capability and compounds at every stage.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Given this strategy, NVIDIA designs its models with a focus on efficiency and speed. The following design choices are what make these models both fast and capable. The first two make the model faster and more efficient. The last one makes it more capable.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>1. The hybrid architecture</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most well-known models are built almost entirely on the Transformer’s attention mechanism. Attention lets every token in the input look at every other token, which is powerful for capturing relationships but expensive. The cost grows with the square of the input length, so doubling the input roughly quadruples the work. The model has to keep every earlier token in memory as it runs. On very long inputs, that gets slow and costly.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The other main class is the state space model, and Mamba is its best-known example. Instead of comparing every token with every other one, a Mamba layer reads the sequence once and compresses everything it has seen into a fixed-size memory. That makes it cheap: the cost grows linearly with length, and the memory stays constant no matter how long the input. The tradeoff is that a fixed-size memory cannot keep every detail, so Mamba is weaker at recalling one exact fact buried far back.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" swapped</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>NVIDIA’s models rely on the same hybrid pattern. style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On top of the hybrid design, the models also use mixture-of-experts, or MoE, layers. An MoE layer consists of many small expert layers and routes each token to only a few of them. So instead of running every parameter on every token, the model activates only a small subset of its parameters. That allows us to use a large total capacity at a low per-token cost, which keeps the model fast.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: sequence. Attention can always go back and find an exact fact. Put together, they are smarter than either one alone. NVIDIA published this hybrid result in 2024, and other labs, including the teams behind Qwen and Kimi, have since moved in the same direction.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>2. Co-designing the GPU and the model</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The second choice is where NVIDIA’s two businesses meet. Its larger models are pretrained in a 4-bit number format called NVFP4, meaning most of the math during training uses just four bits per value. Fewer bits means less memory and less data to move, so the math runs faster and on less power.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Note that four bits is very little precision. Most teams train in higher precision and only shrink the model afterward, which loses accuracy. NVIDIA trained in 4 bits from the first step because it knew its next GPU generation, Blackwell, was being built with fast 4-bit hardware. The model and the chip were designed for each other.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The VP described the mindset behind it. Moore’s law is no longer giving easy gains every generation, so progress has to come from designing the model and the hardware together. The team only attempted 4-bit pretraining because it believed the result was possible. In his words, the first step to inventing something amazing is believing that you can.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>3. Post-training: learning from experience</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With those efficiency choices in place, post-training is where the model gains its capability.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The post-training recipe itself is what most other teams converged to. It starts with supervised fine-tuning, where the model learns from curated examples of good answers and picks up the format and behavior expected of it. Then it switches to reinforcement learning, where the model practices on real tasks and is rewarded for reaching the right outcome. Instead of learning from examples, it learns from its own attempts.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Scaling up this reinforcement learning stage has been shown to improve a model’s capability significantly. Here NVIDIA’s efficiency focus pays off again. Because its models are cheaper to run, it can scale RL at a lower cost, letting the model practice across many environments in parallel and learn from over a million rollouts.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is where the VP placed the real bottleneck for better models. Not data or compute. The diversity of these training environments. The more varied the situations a model practices in, the more capable it becomes, because that is where it gains real problem-solving experience.</span></p><div style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So far we have looked at design decisions to build a model and what is involved to train a single frontier model. But how do they build so many models, and keep improving them so quickly?</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>One Unified Foundation</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Building strong models in one domain is hard. Building them across language, video, robotics, vehicles, and biology needs huge engineering and compute resources. NVIDIA’s approach is to identify a reusable foundation, build it once, and reuse it across different efforts.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The VP traced this back to CUDA, the software layer that made NVIDIA’s GPUs programmable. The “U” stands for Unified, and he called it the most important letter. The idea is to build one foundation and run everything on top of it, rather than maintaining many separate stacks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The same instinct shapes the models. The hybrid architecture from the last section is not rebuilt for each model. The same backbone scales across all three Nemotron sizes. Whole components cross between efforts too. Cosmos Reason, the model built to reason about the physical world, was reused as the reasoning core inside NVIDIA’s Isaac GR00T foundation model, so the robotics team did not have to build that part from scratch. The alternative, ten parallel efforts each reinventing the same pieces, would spread people and compute too thin. According to Bryan, NVIDIA tries to be as lazy as possible, because that is how it gets the most out of limited resources.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The other reason the team is so productive and iterates quickly is cultural. NVIDIA is mostly not top-down; it is a company of volunteers, where teams choose what to work on, and unification happens through invitation rather than control. The culture of collaboration is that if teams work with each other and get more done, they will get more resources than if they each go alone. When everyone shares that belief, a small group can produce a lot.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Open is More Than Just Releasing Weights</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You may have heard a lot about open models. Several AI labs released capable models. You can download the weights and use them. But that is not truly an open model. This is where NVIDIA’s approach really separates it from the other labs. As Bryan puts it, Nemotron is not just a model. It is also the data, the tools, the training recipes, and the ideas published in the papers. The finished weights are just the last step.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;">Open weights alone are not really open</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In practice that means NVIDIA publishes the training datasets, the post-training datasets, the reinforcement learning environments, and the recipes needed to reproduce the work. A team can not only run the model, but also see how it was built and train their own version.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The same is true for robotics and self-driving cars, where developers can use open source simulation and learning frameworks, datasets to train and evaluate the model performance before deployment.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Releasing data at this scale is unusual. It is a scary thing for a company to do. NVIDIA does it anyway, and even shares clever building blocks like synthetic “persona” data that is statistically realistic but fully private, so a model can learn about the world without memorizing real people.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You can see this in what the community has done with it. NVIDIA’s open data and models have spawned a large set of community fine-tunes and derivatives. One of its robotics datasets became one of the most-downloaded datasets on Hugging Face. Many variants of its Nemotron models have millions of downloads each, and the Nemotron family recently crossed 100M in total. You cannot build like that from the weights alone.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Why a Chip Company Gives It All Away</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You may think releasing open models sounds great. But why would a company that sells GPUs give away the AI that runs on them?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Bryan shared two reasons. The first is that NVIDIA needs to understand AI deeply to build the right hardware for it. To design future chips, you have to know where AI is going. The best way to really know is to build models yourself and put them in front of real users. A model kept private is easy to fool yourself about, so releasing it openly keeps the work honest and keeps NVIDIA’s researchers connected to the wider community they learn from. With open models being such a hot topic, the real value is in enabling developers to post-train these models themselves at a fraction of the cost.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The second reason is about the business. NVIDIA grows whenever AI grows. Its goal is to support the ecosystem, not to compete with the companies building on top of it. Every team that adopts open models and builds its own AI can become a future customer for compute. So the company would rather hand the ecosystem the models and let the world’s demand for AI pull its business forward.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: Open technology tends to be safer because more people can inspect it and find problems, the way the open internet is hardened by everyone who uses it.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>What NVIDIA Has Learned Shipping Open Models</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Shipping this many models in public teaches lessons that closed labs never face. Bryan shared several valuable lessons.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0
